subtitleNullable: Monthly US prices for 74 everyday items: eggs, milk, beef, coffee, gas
descriptionNullable:
What everyday things actually cost in the US, month by month: a dozen eggs, a gallon of milk, a pound of ground beef, a gallon of gas, a kilowatt-hour of electricity.

74 items, monthly, January 2015 to July 2026, from the US Bureau of Labor Statistics Average Price Data programme. These are real recorded average transaction prices, not an index - the numbers are in dollars, so you can read them directly.

FILES
- us_average_prices_monthly.csv (8,869 rows) - long: one row per item-month. Start here.
- us_average_prices_wide.csv (139 rows) - wide: one row per month, one column per item. Easy correlations.
- us_average_prices_item_summary.csv (74 rows) - one row per item: coverage, min/max, and change over time.

A STARTING RESULT
Between the first 12 months and the most recent 12 months, every one of the 60 still-published items got more expensive. Not one fell. Median rise +44%. By category: Beef +57%, Energy +55%, Vegetables +41%, Bakery and grains +27%, Dairy +21%, Fruit +16%, Eggs +10%. Coffee is the biggest single riser at +96% - it roughly doubled.

READ THIS BEFORE YOU RANK ANYTHING
1. Do not compare one first month against one last month. Many items are seasonal (lettuce, tomatoes, oranges), so a single month is partly just the time of year. Every change figure here is computed between 12-MONTH AVERAGES at each end, which cancels the seasonality.

2. Series start and stop at different dates. Four items with under 24 months of history were dropped because they cannot support a trend. Of what remains, 60 of 74 are still being published; the rest stop between 2019 and 2022. pct_change_12mo_avg is deliberately NULL for discontinued series, so you never compare a 2019 price to a 2026 one and call it a trend. Filter on is_current for live series only.

3. Eggs are the cautionary tale. Their 12-month-average change is a mild +9.5%, but the monthly series runs from $1.20 (June 2019) to $6.23 (March 2025) - a five-fold swing driven by avian influenza. Any single-endpoint summary of eggs is close to meaningless, which is exactly why the monthly file is the one to analyse.

4. These are nominal prices. Nothing is inflation-adjusted; US CPI-U rose 38.7% over this window, so an item up less than that got cheaper in real terms.

5. National averages only. "U.S. city average" hides large regional differences, and these average across brands, package sizes and stores.

SOURCE AND LICENSE
US Bureau of Labor Statistics, Average Price Data (AP), U.S. city average, monthly, not seasonally adjusted. Built from ap.series plus ap.data.3.Food, ap.data.2.Gasoline and ap.data.1.HouseholdFuels, filtered to area_code 0000 (national). Works of the US federal government are in the public domain (CC0). BLS does not endorse this compilation.
